newsitem.title: UK: Conservatives in civil war over Europe - Blair.
newsitem.headline: Conservatives in civil war over Europe - Blair.

text.p: Election rivals locked horns on Sunday over Britain's role in Europe, with opposition Labour leader Tony Blair saying "civil war" had broken out in the ruling Conservative party over how much sovereignty should be conceded to Brussels.
Prime Minister John Major accused Blair of surrendering to Brussels in advance.
The latest opinion polls in the run-up to the May 1 election showed Labour with a lead of 14 to 19 points over the Conservatives.
Major, bidding to give the ruling party their fifth election win in a row, said Labour showed a Stalinist refusal to allow dissent.
Both leaders have adopted a "wait and see" stance on whether Britain should join a European single currency, but Blair argues that the Conservatives are hopelessly divided on the issue.

"Eleven days out from an election, the Conservatives are in a state of civil war," said Blair, the modernising centrist who has dumped much of Labour's socialist dogma in a bid to end 18 years of opposition.
"The civil war in the Conservative Party has done enormous damage to Britain's national interests," he told BBC Radio.
Paddy Ashdown, leader of the centrist Liberal Democrats, echoed Blair's warnings, claiming the Conservatives were in "meltdown" and incapable of governing effectively.

In a campaign marked by many bitter personal jibes, Blair praised Major for being dogged and tenacious in his turbulent six-year premiership, but said: "It has always been a fight for a job and not for a vision."
Major has been dogged by Conservative party mutinies over Europe with his own stance moving increasingly towards the Eurosceptic camp, which fears Brussels encroaching on national sovereignty.
The Conservatives last week depicted Blair as a ventriloquist's dummy on the knee of German Chancellor Helmut Kohl in a campaign advertisement that party grandees condemned.
"It is insulting to our allies and stirs up anti-German feeling in this country," said former Conservative Prime Minister Edward Heath.
But Major defended the advertisement on Sunday, saying "Politics is a robust trade".
Standing firm on his stance over Europe, he told a Scottish radio phone-in: "If you went into a single currency and it failed, the damage is almost beyond calculation."
Sunday media reports said pro-European finance minister Kenneth Clarke would be keen to join any contest to succeed Major should he step down after the election.
From the Eurosceptic wing of the badly divided party, he could face challenges from defence minister Michael Portillo and Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard.

Clarke forcefully defended the "wait-and-see" currency position, telling BBC Television: "Until we know which countries are joining, the state of their economies and on what basis they are going to run a single monetary policy, it is not in the national interest to make a decision."
But he insisted: "I am flatly against handing over control of tax to Europe, flatly against handing over control of public spending to Europe. So is every European finance minister I know."
